1.note: Zechariah is using the term **Behold** to focus the attention of his listeners on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully]

Zechariah is using **a day is coming for Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the time is coming when Yahweh will act to judge his enemies and rescue his people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time of Yahweh’s judgment is near]

Zechariah is speaking to the city of Jerusalem, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what will happen to the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [and the spoil taken from Jerusalem will be divided within that city]
The pronoun **your** refers to Jerusalem which (see verse 2) represents the people in Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

The expression **will be divided** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your enemies will divide your spoil in your midst]
The word **your** is singular here because Zechariah is addressing the city of Jerusalem, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

2.note: Yahweh is speaking here. If it would be helpful in your language, you could that make clear. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh says, “I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem]

2.q: וְ⁠נִלְכְּדָ֣ה הָ⁠עִ֗יר וְ⁠נָשַׁ֨סּוּ֙ הַ⁠בָּ֣תִּ֔ים וְ⁠הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֖ים תשגלנה
2.note: The expressions **will be captured**, **will be plundered**, and **will be raped** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the nations will capture the city, and they will plunder the houses, and they will rape the women]

The oral reading tradition of the original language substitutes a less explicit word here, referring in a polite way to what the soldiers will do to **the women**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and the women will be violated]

Here, **the city** represents “the people who live in the city.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And half of the city’s inhabitants will go out into the exile]
The fraction **half** means one part out of two equal parts of the people of the city. Alternate translation: [one of every two people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **exile**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be forced to live in a foreign land]

Zechariah is speaking as if the rest of the people would literally ** not be cut off** from the city. He means that the enemies will not remove them from it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the rest of the people will remain in the city]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **cut off**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [the rest of the people will remain in the city]

Habakkuk uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the half of the city that will go into exile and the rest of the people who will remain. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, the rest of the people]

3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh fought powerfully for his people **on a day of battle** in the past, so he will fight against these nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as he fought powerfully for his people in past battles]

4.note: Zechariah is using **his feet**, one part of Yahweh, to represent all of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will stand]

Zechariah is using **on that day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at the time when Yahweh will act to judge the nations and rescue his people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on that day of judgment and deliverance]

Here, **the face of Jerusalem** represents “the area in front of Jerusalem.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which is in front of Jerusalem on the east]

4.q: וְ⁠נִבְקַע֩ הַ֨ר הַ⁠זֵּיתִ֤ים מֵֽ⁠חֶצְי⁠וֹ֙ מִזְרָ֣חָ⁠ה וָ⁠יָ֔מָּ⁠ה
4.note: The expression **will be split** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Mount of Olives will split apart down the middle, from east to west, forming]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [creating a very great valley]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and its other half will move away toward the south]

5.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the valley of the mountains will reach to Azal, you will flee by the valley of my mountains]
The word **Azal** is the name of a place.

Zechariah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the earthquake that terrified you]

The implication is that this was a well-known earthquake that the people of Judah still remembered. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the days of Uzziah the king of Judah, that earthquake everyone remembers]

6.note: Zechariah is not using the phrase translated as **And it will happen on that day** to introduce a new event. In this and in the several following verses, he is using **on that day** to refer back to the appointed day introduced in verse 1. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for looking back to the same day. Alternate translation: [And it will happen on that same day]

Zechariah is using the adjective **splendid** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the splendid heavenly bodies]

The implication is that the normal sources of light will fail on that day. This could mean: (1) that there will be no light and that instead there will be cold and frost, Alternate translation: [there will not be light; instead there will be cold and frost] or (2) that the bright heavenly bodies will no longer shine. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the sun, moon, and stars will stop shining]

7.note: The expression **will be known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will know about it]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it will not be day and it will not be night]

Zechariah is using the two parts of a full day, **day** and **night**, to mean the entire cycle of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [unlike any ordinary period of time]

Zechariah states **And it will happen** here to indicate a contrast between the darkness that would normally be expected at evening and the light that will be present instead. In your translation, do not try to explain or fix this contract, instead indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [there will be neither day nor night, but at the time of evening there will be light]

8.note: Zechariah is using the two main seasons of the year, **the summer** and **the winter**, to mean the whole year. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all year long]

Zechariah is using **living waters** as a common expression of the culture to mean “fresh water that flows continually” and “water that gives life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continually flowing fresh streams] or [life-giving water]

9.note: The implication is that people everywhere will worship Yahweh alone and honor him alone as God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will be the only God whom people worship, and his name, the only name that they honor]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that his name will be one, that is, unique. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his name will be one, meaning unique]

Here, **his name** represents Yahweh himself and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his reputation will be unique]

10.note: Zechariah is using the two extremes of the land of Judah, **Geba** in the north and **Rimmon** in the south, to mean all of the land between them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from one end of the land to the other]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the Arabah** is a flat plain, so the land around Jerusalem will become flat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [All the land will become as flat as the Arabah plain]

The pronoun **it** refers to Jerusalem, not to the land that will become flat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But Jerusalem will rise up and will dwell in its place]

10.q: לְ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁ֣עַר בִּנְיָמִ֗ן עַד־מְק֞וֹם שַׁ֤עַר הָֽ⁠רִאשׁוֹן֙ עַד־שַׁ֣עַר הַ⁠פִּנִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִגְדַּ֣ל חֲנַנְאֵ֔ל עַ֖ד יִקְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
10.note: The words **the Gate of Benjamin**, **the First Gate**, **the Gate of the Corners**, and **the Tower of Hananel** are the names of places in Jerusalem.

10.q: לְ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁ֣עַר בִּנְיָמִ֗ן עַד־מְק֞וֹם שַׁ֤עַר הָֽ⁠רִאשׁוֹן֙ עַד־שַׁ֣עַר הַ⁠פִּנִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִגְדַּ֣ל חֲנַנְאֵ֔ל עַ֖ד יִקְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
10.note: Zechariah is referring to all of Jerusalem by naming two extremes, **the Gate of Benjamin** and **the winepresses of the king**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the whole city]

11.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Jerusalem, and the pronoun **it** refers to the city of Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And her people will dwell in Jerusalem]

The implication is that enemies will never again devote Jerusalem to complete destruction in war. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and no enemy will ever again devote it to destruction]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and no one will destroy it again]

**Jerusalem** is spoken of as a living thing. By referring to the city in this way, the meaning is that its name represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Jerusalem will dwell in security]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Jerusalem will dwell securely]

12.q: בְּשָׂר֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠הוּא֙ עֹמֵ֣ד עַל־רַגְלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠עֵינָי⁠ו֙ תִּמַּ֣קְנָה בְ⁠חֹֽרֵי⁠הֶ֔ן וּ⁠לְשׁוֹנ֖⁠וֹ תִּמַּ֥ק בְּ⁠פִי⁠הֶֽם
12.note: The pronouns **he** and **his** refer to each individual among the peoples who waged war against Jerusalem, while the pronoun **their** refers to those same peoples together as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [each person’s flesh will rot away while he is standing on his feet, and his eyes will rot in their sockets, and his tongue will rot in his mouth]

Zechariah is using **while he is standing on his feet** as a common expression of the culture to mean “while he is still alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while he is yet living]

13.note: Zechariah is using the possessive form **a great tumult of Yahweh** to describe a tumult that Yahweh himself will cause. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a great tumult that Yahweh sends]

Here the masculine term **man** could refer to: (1) soldiers of the enemy armies, Alternate translation: [and each soldier will seize the hand of his neighbor] or (2) have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and each person will seize the hand of his neighbor]

Zechariah is using **each man will seize the hand of his neighbor** as a common expression of the culture to mean that people will panic and attack one another in confusion. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone will grab hold of the person next to them in panic] or [everyone will turn against the person next to them in confusion]

Zechariah is using **his hand will go up against** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will attack.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will attack his neighbor]

14.note: The implication is that the people of Judah will take part in this battle. This could mean: (1) that they will fight at Jerusalem alongside its people against the nations. Alternate translation: [And also Judah will join Jerusalem in fighting against the nations] or (2) that they will fight against Jerusalem along with the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Judah will also join the nations in fighting against Jerusalem]

The expression **will be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they will collect the wealth of all the nations around]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in extremely large amounts]

15.note: Zechariah is using the possessive form **the plague of the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey** to describe the plague that will strike those animals. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the plague that will strike the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey]

Zechariah is not referring to a specific **horse**, **mule**, **camel**, or **donkey**. He means horses, mules, camels, and donkeys in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the horses, mules, camels, and donkeys]

16.note: Bowing down before someone was a symbolic action by which a person showed honor and submission to a ruler. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [to bow down in honor and submission to the King]

The **Festival of Booths** is a kind of yearly celebration during which the Israelites lived in temporary shelters for a week to remember how their ancestors lived after they came out of Egypt. If your readers would not be familiar with what the Festival of Booths is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the yearly festival of living in temporary huts]

17.q: אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא־יַעֲלֶ֜ה מֵ⁠אֵ֨ת מִשְׁפְּח֤וֹת הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙ אֶל־יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לְ⁠הִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֔ת לְ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת וְ⁠לֹ֥א עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם יִהְיֶ֥ה הַ⁠גָּֽשֶׁם
17.note: Zechariah is presenting a possible condition, that some of the clans of the earth will not go up to Jerusalem to worship Yahweh. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [if any of the clans of the earth do not go up to Jerusalem to bow down to the King, Yahweh of Armies, then on them there will not be the rain]

The implication is that without rain the crops of those people will fail, and so this will be a punishment for them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on them there will not be the rain, and as a punishment their crops will not grow]

18.note: The terms **does not go up** and **does not come** mean similar things. Zechariah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [does not come at all]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh will judge Egypt by plague instead of withholding rain, since rain is not how Egypt grows crops. See the UST. (2) Yahweh will also withhold rain from southern Egypt that feeds the Nile River that the people of Egypt water their crops from rather than from direct rain. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then the rain will not replenish the Nile either]

19.q: זֹ֥את תִּהְיֶ֖ה חַטַּ֣את מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ⁠חַטַּאת֙ כָּל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם
19.note: Here, **the sin** represents the punishment for sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [This will be the punishment of Egypt and the punishment of all the nations]

20.note: The implication is that things which were very common will become holy. Someone will engrave the words “Holy to Yahweh” on the bells, just as those words were engraved on the turban of the high priest. To transfer something so holy to something so common would have been somewhat shocking to the original audience. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on the common bells of the horse, someone will carve an inscription reading, “Holy to Yahweh]

20.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֤ה הַ⁠סִּירוֹת֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה כַּ⁠מִּזְרָקִ֖ים לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּֽחַ
20.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the bowls** that the priests use at the altar are sacred, so **the pots in the house of Yahweh** will be sacred. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the pots in the house of Yahweh will be just as holy as the bowls that are before the altar]

Here, **the face of the altar** represents “the front of the altar.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the altar]

21.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the pots in Jerusalem and in Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and will take a few of those pots and will boil their sacrifices in them]

Zechariah is not referring to a specific **Canaanite**. He means Canaanites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any Canaanites]

Here, **a Canaanite** represents someone who does not belong in the house of Yahweh. You may wish to add a footnote here with the meaning you do not choose. This could mean: (1) a trader or merchant, since the Canaanites were well known as traders, Alternate translation: [there will not be a trader again in the house of Yahweh of Armies] or (2) an unclean foreigner. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [there will not be a unclean foreigner again in the house of Yahweh of Armies]
